AB-01.c01: An air brake system is really **3 braking systems**: service (brake pedal), parking (parking brake control) and emergency (stops you if the brake system fails).
To count as air brakes for your CDL, the vehicle needs **air gauges** and **low pressure warning device(s)**.
If your road-test vehicle lacks them, you get the **"L" (No Air Brakes)** restriction on your CDL.
[CA] A full service brake application must send **at least 90 percent** of the remaining tank pressure to every brake chamber.
AB-01.c02: The **air compressor** pumps air into the storage tanks; the engine drives it through gears or a v-belt.
If the compressor has its own oil supply, **check its oil level** before driving.
The governor stops the compressor at **cut-out, around 125 psi**, and restarts it at **cut-in, around 100 psi**.
For a governor question use 125 cut-out / 100 cut-in; the leakage test's **120–140 psi** cut-out range also counts as normal.
AB-01.c03: Air tanks hold enough air to use the brakes **several times** even if the compressor stops working.
Water and compressor oil collect in the tank bottoms; the water can **freeze** in cold weather and cause **brake failure**.
Manual drains open with a **quarter turn** or a pulled cable; drain them completely **at the end of each day** of driving.
An **alcohol evaporator** cuts the risk of ice in brake valves; check and fill it **every day in cold weather**.
The evaporator does **not** replace draining; you still drain daily unless the tanks have automatic drains.
AB-01.c04: The **safety valve** sits in the first tank and usually opens at **150 psi** to protect against too much pressure.
If the safety valve lets air out, **something is wrong**; have a mechanic fix it.
The brake pedal (foot valve or treadle valve) sends **more air** to the brakes the harder you push.
**Pumping the pedal** for no reason can let air out faster than the compressor replaces it; if pressure gets too low, the brakes will not work.
AB-01.c05: Foundation brakes are at each wheel; the most common type is the **S-cam drum brake**.
S-cam order: air enters the brake chamber → push rod → **slack adjuster** → camshaft → S-cam spreads the shoes against the drum.
A **return spring** pulls the shoes off the drum when you release; braking makes heat, and too much heat can make brakes stop working.
**CamLaster** has a built-in adjustment system; **wedge** brakes drive a wedge between shoes; **disc** brakes use a power screw to clamp the rotor.
Wedge and disc brakes are **less common** than S-cam brakes.
AB-01.c06: The **supply pressure gauge** shows tank pressure; a dual system has one gauge per half or one gauge with **2 needles**.
The **application pressure gauge** shows air going to the brakes; needing more to hold the same speed means **brake fade**, so slow down and use a lower gear.
A visible low-air warning must come on between **55 and 75 psi** (older vehicles: ½ of governor cut-out); large buses commonly at **80–85 psi**.
A manual reset **wig wag** will not stay up until pressure is above **55 psi**.
The **stop light switch**, an electric switch worked by air pressure, turns on the brake lights.
AB-01.c07: Some vehicles made **before 1975** have a front brake limiting valve with "normal" and "slippery" settings.
"Slippery" cuts front brake air pressure **in half** and reduces your stopping power.
Front wheel braking is good in all conditions; front skids are not likely even on ice, so keep the control in **"normal"**.
Automatic limiting valves give full front air only at **60 psi or more** application pressure; the driver cannot control them.
AB-01.c08: Trucks, tractors and buses must have parking and emergency brakes held on by **mechanical force**, because air can leak away.
**Spring brakes** are held back by air pressure; take the air away (parking control or a leak) and the springs put the brakes on.
Tractor and straight truck spring brakes come fully on at **20–45 psi** (typically 20–30 psi).
Don't wait for them; **stop safely** as soon as the low-air warning comes on, while the service brakes still work.
Out-of-adjustment brakes mean **neither** the regular nor the parking/emergency brakes work right.
AB-01.c09: Newer vehicles use a **yellow, diamond-shaped** knob: **pull out** = parking brakes on, push in = off; older vehicles may use a lever.
**Never press the brake pedal** while the spring brakes are on; springs plus air pressure can damage the brakes.
A **modulating control valve** applies spring brakes gradually; to park, move the lever as far as it goes and lock it.
Dual parking control valves use a separate tank to release spring brakes, but it has air for **only a few times**, so plan carefully.
AB-01.c10: **ABS** keeps wheels from locking up in hard braking.
Required on air-brake truck tractors built on or after **March 1, 1997**, and other air-brake vehicles on or after **March 1, 1998**.
The ABS malfunction lamp is **yellow**: on the instrument panel, or on the trailer's left side; older lamps may stay on until over **5 mph**.
A lamp that stays on after the bulb check, or comes on while driving, means you may have **lost ABS control** at one or more wheels.
ABS does **not** change normal braking power or necessarily shorten stops; it helps you **keep control**.
